hints: Start by thinking about the word set. A human body cell has two versions of each chromosome, one from each parent, while a gamete has only one version.
Now link this to the symbols n and 2n. One complete set is described as n, so what does two complete sets mean for the definitions?
walkthrough:
Think in Sets, Not Numbers**
Think of chromosomes as coming in sets. In humans, one set is 23 different chromosomes. A gamete carries just that one set, so it can contribute half the genetic material at fertilisation.

Build Both Definitions Clearly**
Haploid means having one complete set. Diploid means having two complete sets, usually one maternal and one paternal set together. That is why diploid is 2n and haploid is n, and why meiosis must halve the number of sets.
Final answer: Haploid is one complete set of chromosomes (n); diploid is two complete sets of chromosomes (2n).

hints: Start with prophase I. What must long, thin chromatin do to become visible, and what do matching maternal and paternal chromosomes do together?
For metaphase I, picture pairs rather than single chromosomes. Where in the cell do pairs line up, and how is their orientation decided?
For anaphase I, remember this is different from mitosis and meiosis II. Which structures separate - sister chromatids or whole homologous chromosomes?
For telophase I, follow the chromosomes to the end of this first division. Where do they arrive and what happens to their condensed state?
walkthrough:
Prophase I - Condense and Pair Up**
Chromatin condenses to become short, thick visible chromosomes. Then homologous chromosomes, one maternal and one paternal of each type, pair up side by side to form bivalents. This pairing is called synapsis and allows crossing over with chiasmata formation.

Metaphase I - Pairs on the Equator**
The bivalents line up on the metaphase plate at the equator, attached to spindle fibres. The orientation of each maternal and paternal homologue facing each pole is random, so this gives independent assortment of homologous pairs.

Anaphase I - Homologues Separate**
One whole chromosome from each homologous pair moves to opposite poles. Note the key point: sister chromatids stay together here, so it is homologous chromosomes that separate. This is the reduction step that halves the chromosome number.

Telophase I - Arrive and Unwind**
The separated chromosomes, still consisting of two chromatids, reach opposite poles of the cell. They then decondense back toward chromatin. The cell is now ready to divide into two haploid cells before meiosis II.

Final answer: Prophase I: chromosomes condense and homologous chromosomes pair to form bivalents, with crossing over/chiasmata formation. Metaphase I: bivalents line up on the equator with independent assortment. Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles. Telophase I: chromosomes reach opposite poles and decondense.

hints: Nuclear division divides the chromosomes, but a separate term beginning with cyto- is used for splitting the cytoplasm and organelles into two cells.
walkthrough:
Separate Nucleus from Cytoplasm**
Meiosis describes nuclear division. The physical splitting of the cytoplasm, organelles and cell membrane to form two separate daughter cells is called cytokinesis. In animal cells this happens by constriction of the cell surface.
